summary: Describes the Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP), which connects multiple IPv4 PIM Sparse-Mode domains. Each domain keeps its own Rendezvous Point and need not depend on those of other domains. The RFC is experimental and documents what existing MSDP implementations already do.

plainLanguage.summary: Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP) lets separate multicast domains announce active sources to one another. A domain can keep its own Rendezvous Point and join a source tree only when one of its receivers wants that source.

questions: how do pim sm domains share multicast sources
how do pim domains discover multicast sources
subtitle: How multicast source announcements connect separate PIM-SM domains.

tldr.problem: Receivers in one PIM Sparse-Mode domain need to discover active sources in another domain without depending on that domain's Rendezvous Point.
tldr.mechanism: Rendezvous Points exchange Source-Active messages over TCP. A receiving RP that has interested members joins the source tree, while peer-RPF checks control how announcements are forwarded.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3618 is Experimental and documents existing MSDP implementations. It describes use between PIM domains and between Anycast-RPs.

today: RFC 3618 is an Experimental RFC from October 2003, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document says it reflects existing MSDP implementations.

sections.title: Connecting PIM-SM Domains
sections.content:
MSDP connects IPv4 Protocol Independent Multicast Sparse-Mode (PIM-SM) domains. Each domain can use its own Rendezvous Point (RP), without depending on RPs in other domains.

MSDP peers exchange control information over Transmission Control Protocol (TCP). The peer network lets domains discover sources; if a domain has receivers interested in a source, PIM-SM builds a source tree to deliver its multicast data.
sections.plainLanguage: Each domain keeps its own RP and exchanges source information with other domains. A domain joins the data-delivery path when one of its receivers wants a source.

sections.title: Source-Active Announcements and Joining
sections.content:
When an RP learns of a new source, it sends a Source-Active (SA) message to its MSDP peers. The message identifies the source, multicast group and originating RP. Only RPs originate SA messages; intermediate speakers may forward messages from other domains.

A receiving RP checks whether its domain has members for the announced group. If so, it joins the source tree toward the source. This flood-and-join procedure lets an RP with no interested receivers ignore an announcement. Speakers cache SA messages to reduce repeated forwarding and help new receivers join promptly.
sections.plainLanguage: An RP announces a new source and the group receiving its data. Other RPs join the source tree only when their own domains have interested receivers.

sections.title: Peer-RPF Checks and Mesh Groups
sections.content:
A peer reverse-path-forwarding (peer-RPF) check uses the RP address in an SA message and the multicast routing information base to decide which peer should have sent it. A speaker accepts an SA only when it arrives from that selected peer; otherwise it drops the message. Accepted messages are forwarded to other peers.

A mesh group can reduce duplicate flooding among fully meshed peers. A member accepts an SA from another member but must not forward it to the other members, because the originator has already sent it to them. The RFC says an SA must not cross an administrative scope boundary for its multicast group.
sections.plainLanguage: A router checks whether an announcement came from the expected direction before forwarding it. Mesh-group members avoid repeating announcements to peers that already received them.

sections.title: Peer Connections and Message Format
sections.content:
MSDP uses TCP port 639. In a peering relationship, the peer with the higher IP address listens and the other peer initiates the connection. Keepalive messages and timers help detect whether the connection remains active.

Messages use a Type-Length-Value format. An IPv4 Source-Active message is type 1 and carries an RP address plus one or more source-and-group entries. The maximum TLV length is 9192 octets; the RFC also defines a KeepAlive TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: Peers establish a TCP connection and exchange short messages with a type, length and value. The main message lists active source-and-group pairs.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Notes
sections.content:
An MSDP implementation must support Keyed MD5 to protect control messages and must interoperate with peers that do not support it. The RFC recommends filters and limits to reduce state growth during denial-of-service attacks.

The document describes MSDP primarily between PIM domains and between Anycast-RPs within one domain. It is an Experimental protocol document that records existing implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: MSDP peers can protect control messages with Keyed MD5. Filters and limits can help prevent too many source announcements from consuming state.
